summary: Young children (around 5-6) quantify capacity by repeated filling and pouring with IDENTICAL units: counting how many cupfuls fill a container (non-standard units), then meeting the litre and a marked measuring jug (standard units), recording each result as a number + unit ('4 cups', '2 litres'). The core insight — shared with length and mass — is the inverse relationship: a bigger cup means FEWER cupfuls fill the same container. Reading a marked vessel means valuing its intervals, not just counting marks. Real water play is the natural companion to any screen model.
misconceptions: Uses different-sized cups yet counts 'more cupfuls = holds more' (unit-size ignorance)
Fills cups inconsistently (part-full) but counts them as equal
Reads a measuring jug by marks rather than intervals; misjudges a level between graduations
Loses count or spills, then reports the count anyway

activities.title: Fill, count, record — then swap the cup
steps: Fill a container cupful by cupful using identical cups, filling each cup to the same mark or brim, and keep a running count (e.g. pour until the count climbs to 8).
Record the result as a number and unit, e.g. 'the jug = 8 cups'.
Now fill the SAME container again using a bigger cup, filling each to the brim, and count again (e.g. this time only 4).
Say out loud what changed: the container didn't change, so why did the count change? Record 'the jug = 4 big cups'.
Estimate first, then check by filling, for a new container.
activities.insight: The same container needs fewer cupfuls when the cup is bigger — a larger unit gives a smaller count (inverse relationship) — and a capacity measurement is only meaningful when the units are identical and consistently filled.

activities.title: Read the measuring jug by its intervals
steps: Work out what one interval on the jug is worth: find two labelled whole-litre marks, count the equal spaces between them, and share the litre between them (e.g. if one unlabelled line sits halfway between the 0 and 1 litre marks, there are two equal spaces, so each space is worth half a litre and that line marks half a litre).
Read the water level to the nearest interval and say how much water is in the jug.
Practise with a level that falls between two graduations and judge the nearest mark.
Explain how you knew a particular line means half a litre — justify it from the spacing you counted, don't just count lines.
Introduce the litre as a standard unit and record readings with number + unit.
activities.insight: A measuring vessel is read by valuing the spaces (intervals) between marks against the level, not by simply counting lines — the same skill as reading a ruler or dial.

activities.title: Practice and check: cupful counts, jug reading, and ordering
steps: Complete fill-in items such as 'the jug = ___ cupfuls' after a filling activity.
Answer 'read the measuring jug' items where you identify the level to the nearest interval.
Decide whether a bigger cup needs MORE or FEWER cupfuls to fill the same container, and explain why.
Answer the probe: 'You needed 4 big cups but 8 small cups for the same jug — how can it be both?' and 'If you filled the jug with a tiny egg-cup instead of a mug, would you need more or fewer? Why?'
activities.insight: Secure that identical units and the inverse relationship govern capacity counts, and that jug readings depend on interval value — able to apply these to fresh cases.

checkQuestion: Give the child a jug to fill, a set of identical small cups, a larger cup, and a measuring jug marked in intervals. Watch how they work: (1) 'Use this cup to find how many cupfuls fill this jug.' (2) 'Priya used a bigger cup to fill the same jug — will she need more cupfuls or fewer? Why?' (3) 'Read this measuring jug — how much water is in it?'
checkAnswer: (1) Fills with consistently-full identical cups and reports 'N cupfuls', recording the unit. (2) FEWER cupfuls, because a bigger cup holds more so fewer of them fill the same jug (inverse relationship). (3) Reads the jug by valuing the intervals to the water level.
